title: Estimating the Net Value of Cleaning a Rooftop Photovoltaic Array
text:
002  Estimating the Net Value of Cleaning a Rooftop Photovoltaic Array
Abstract: A rise in electricity production after photovoltaic cleaning is an observation, but it is not yet an estimate of the cleaning effect. Weather changes, equipment availability, and the value of additional electricity can alter the interpretation. This paper proposes a simultaneous comparison method for a rooftop system with independently measurable sections. A baseline output ratio estimates the untreated counterfactual, while an explicit cost threshold connects recovered generation to an operational choice. Hypothetical figures illustrate the difference between a positive generation effect and a financially worthwhile intervention. The study is a methodological proposal without field measurements. It identifies the evidence needed to support a cleaning decision and the conditions under which the proposed comparison should be rejected.
Keywords: photovoltaic systems; cleaning; counterfactual; energy yield; maintenance economics
1 A maintenance question with a misleading shortcut
Consider a factory manager who sees higher production on the day after a cleaning visit. The contractor may regard the increase as a demonstration of effectiveness. Yet the previous day could have been cloudy, or the inverter could have spent an hour unavailable. A daily before and after comparison combines these changes with any effect of cleaning. The opposite error is also possible: a cloudy day after cleaning could conceal a real recovery. The relevant question is how much electricity the cleaned section would have produced over the same observation period if it had remained untreated. That quantity is not directly observed.
The distinction between laboratory conversion efficiency and operating energy yield matters here. DOE identifies heat, dirt, and shade among the factors relevant to system output [1]. This supports the need to consider operating conditions; it does not provide a universal recovery percentage for the roof being evaluated. The proposal therefore uses published material to define plausible influences and constructs a site specific comparison to estimate the intervention. Nameplate capacity can normalize sections of different size, but it cannot remove unequal shading, equipment behaviour, or measurement error. The chosen comparison must make those differences sufficiently stable or explicitly model them.
2 Define the boundary before collecting numbers
The first requirement is a measurement boundary that matches the cleaning treatment. Two groups of panels sharing an inseparable output measurement cannot be treated as independently observed sections merely because their positions are different. A useful candidate is a pair of sections with separately recorded output, similar orientation, and similar equipment. The manager should retain their capacities, module types, shading descriptions, and meter specifications. The test need not assume that the sections produce exactly the same amount. It needs a reason to believe that their relationship would remain sufficiently predictable without the intervention.
The observation calendar should include a baseline period before cleaning and a comparison period afterwards. Both sections should be measured on the same clock. Inverter outages, output restrictions, and missing readings require event records. A timestamp shift can make one section appear weak during a changing cloud pattern even if its equipment performs normally. Before defining a sophisticated adjustment, it is worth checking whether the clocks and cumulative meter resets are consistent. A clean table of daily totals can still be built from incompatible intervals. The measurement audit is therefore part of the research method, rather than a minor administrative step.
3 A baseline ratio and its assumptions
Let r0 denote an estimated baseline relationship between the treatment section and the control section during acceptable precleaning intervals. After cleaning, let Ec be control generation during a comparable interval and Et be treatment generation. A simple untreated prediction is r0 × Ec, giving a candidate increment ΔE = Et − r0 × Ec. This is an analytical construction for the proposed study. It assumes that the baseline relationship remains applicable apart from cleaning. If shade moves differently across the two sections, or equipment changes during the test, the resulting increment can mix the treatment with those changes.
The baseline should consequently be examined before the treatment is performed. Plotting ratios across time of day and different operating conditions can reveal a pattern that one average would hide. A stable midday ratio with an unstable morning ratio may justify a narrower evaluation window, provided that window is chosen before the outcomes are inspected. If no stable window exists, a weather and temperature model or a different control is necessary. PVWatts offers a documented performance modelling reference [2]. The present proposal does not claim to reproduce its detailed model, and a generic model should not be substituted for evidence that the selected on site comparison is valid.
4 Hypothetical generation recovery
For illustration, suppose both sections have a capacity of 25 kilowatts and the baseline ratio is 0.97. On one valid postcleaning day, the control section produces 100 kilowatt hours and the cleaned section produces 102 kilowatt hours. The untreated prediction is 97 kilowatt hours, so the candidate recovery is 5 kilowatt hours. Relative to the predicted baseline, this is approximately 5.15 percent. All of these figures are invented for a worked calculation. They are not field observations, and they cannot be used as evidence that cleaning usually restores that proportion of output.
The example also shows why capacity normalization is not sufficient. Both sections have the same rated capacity, but their baseline relationship is not one. Ignoring the ratio would attribute only the two kilowatt hour difference to cleaning. Conversely, using a ratio from an unsuitable period could exaggerate the effect. Recovery should be accumulated across matched valid intervals using the selected prediction method. A total should not quietly include intervals with no control measurement. Where exclusions are necessary, the report should state how much time and generation they cover. A small reported increment can be sensitive to apparently minor exclusions.
5 From electricity to a financial threshold
Suppose a cleaning visit costs 240 currency units. Assume that, without cleaning, the relevant section would generate 3,000 kilowatt hours over the period during which the benefit persists, and that each additional usable kilowatt hour is worth 0.10 currency units. With a constant proportional recovery, the break even recovery fraction is 240 divided by 300, or 80 percent. A recovery of 5.15 percent would be worth approximately 15.46 currency units under these assumptions. The calculation does not show that photovoltaic cleaning is generally uneconomic. It shows that this particular hypothetical combination of cost, generation, price, and duration would not justify the visit on electricity value alone.
Change the persistent baseline generation to 30,000 kilowatt hours and the break even fraction falls to 8 percent. Change the unit value again, and the boundary moves. The sensitivity is important because a visually dirty module does not identify the future monetary gain from cleaning. Neither does an impressive first day percentage identify the duration of that gain. The evaluation should obtain an actual quotation, an appropriate estimate of baseline generation, and a justified period of persistence. A manager can then see which assumption would have to change to reverse the recommendation, instead of receiving a single apparently decisive return estimate.
6 Determine the value of additional production
The value assigned to a kilowatt hour must match how the site uses it. Additional production consumed by the factory can have a different value from electricity exported under a separate agreement. The proposed calculation therefore separates self consumed and exported increments where the metering and contracts permit it. It should not price all recovered generation at the retail purchase tariff by default. Applicable contractual and operating information should be checked for the site; this methodological article does not supply a tariff or a regulatory entitlement. A reported value should carry its date and pricing assumptions.
Equipment or grid constraints can also limit usable recovery. If an interval is already constrained at the relevant output limit, a cleaner module may not translate its potential gain into additional recorded delivery. A comparison based on delivered alternating current electricity should retain that distinction. The report should separately describe technical recovery and monetizable recovery when they differ. The point is not to penalize cleaning for an unrelated restriction. It is to avoid paying for an expected benefit that the operating system cannot realize over the period in question. This is a decision about the whole delivery boundary, not just the panel surface.
7 Test assignment and measurement uncertainty
Where the roof contains several comparable sections, sections can be grouped by known position differences and the first cleaning assignment randomized within each group. Blocking and randomization have established roles in experimental design [3]. In this proposed application, they reduce the risk that an operator always selects the worst or easiest section for treatment. They do not make every hourly observation an independent experiment. Measurements within one section share equipment and weather influences, so hundreds of readings can contain much less independent information than their row count suggests. The analysis must preserve section identity and the assignment procedure.
The reporting plan should state acceptable operating intervals, treatment dates, missing data rules, and primary outcomes before looking at postcleaning gains. Meter precision and baseline prediction error should be considered together. A positive difference smaller than the plausible error cannot support an exact recovery claim. If an inverter failure removes a large part of the observation window, the remaining intervals might not represent normal operation. Such an event should be described rather than hidden. A second analysis using different reasonable handling assumptions can show whether the decision remains stable. This is more informative than reporting several decimal places from uncertain input data.
8 Persistence and broader maintenance costs
The output relationship should be monitored after the initial comparison. Rain may reduce the difference between cleaned and untreated sections, while new deposition may progressively reduce the cleaned section's advantage. The procedure should estimate persistence from records where possible rather than extending the first observation across an entire year. A benefit curve that fades quickly gives a different total value from a persistent recovery of the same initial magnitude. The report should identify the observation end date and distinguish measured persistence from forecast persistence. Forecasts remain hypotheses to be updated as additional records become available.
Costs can include access, water, labour, inspection, downtime, and any applicable equipment requirements. Roof access and electrical work must follow the site's approved procedures and manufacturer conditions; this paper does not provide cleaning instructions. A risk that has not been quantified should not automatically become a zero in the financial model. Conversely, a maintenance intervention required to address a confirmed defect can have a justification beyond short term generation revenue. The report should name that justification separately. Mixing all maintenance purposes into an untraceable percentage makes it impossible to see what evidence supports the decision.
9 Conclusion
A defensible cleaning decision requires an estimate of additional generation, an estimate of its usable value, and a credible duration. The proposed matched comparison addresses the first quantity through a baseline relationship and simultaneously measured control. The cost threshold connects that estimate to an operational choice. Hypothetical calculations demonstrate why a positive recovery can still fail to cover a visit, and why a changed observation period can reverse the result. No site specific recovery has been established here. The next step is a documented on site comparison that can reject the proposed benefit, rather than a before and after total selected because it appears favourable.
References
[1] U.S. Department of Energy. Photovoltaic System Design and Energy Yield. https://www.energy.gov/cmei/systems/photovoltaic-system-design-and-energy-yield Accessed 4 October 2026.
[2] Dobos, A. P. (2014). PVWatts Version 5 Manual. Technical Report NREL/TP-6A20-62641. Golden, Colorado: National Renewable Energy Laboratory. https://docs.nrel.gov/docs/fy14osti/62641.pdf
[3] NIST/SEMATECH. e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, Section 5.3.3.2, Randomized block designs. https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/pri/section3/pri332.htm Accessed 4 October 2026.

title: A Verifiable Idempotency Contract for Order Creation After Network Timeouts
text:
003  A Verifiable Idempotency Contract for Order Creation After Network Timeouts
Abstract: A client timeout cannot establish whether an order creation request failed before execution or succeeded before its response was lost.Retrying without a business identity can create duplicate orders, while refusing all retries can abandon legitimate operations.This design paper specifies a bounded idempotency contract for an order service using one transactional database.It examines intent identifiers, concurrent admission, result replay, retention, and the separate problem of external payment.Event traces and hypothetical fault tests provide logical checks of the proposal; they are not empirical reliability measurements.The central conclusion is that a request identifier is useful only when the database transition and the interface contract make its meaning enforceable.Keywords: order service; idempotency; transactions; network timeout; fault injection
1 The ambiguous outcome
A customer confirms a purchase, and the application sends an order creation request.
The server commits the order, but the connection closes before the response reaches the application.To the customer, this may look identical to a failure before the request reached the server.A second click can therefore represent an attempt to complete the first purchase rather than an intention to purchase again.The application cannot reliably distinguish these possibilities by the appearance of its timeout message.It needs a contract that connects repeated delivery attempts to the same business operation, without collapsing two genuine purchases into one.
RFC 9110 defines idempotency in terms of the intended server effect of repeating a request, and does not generally permit automatic retries of nonidempotent operations without an additional basis [1].An order endpoint implemented with POST does not obtain a business guarantee merely from using HTTP.The proposed guarantee is narrower and testable: for one authenticated customer and one accepted purchase intent, no more than one order is created during the specified retention interval.Delivery attempts and diagnostic log records may occur several times.The contract concerns the order effect, not a fictional promise that the network transmits once.
2 Identify an intention rather than a payload
The client generates an intent identifier when the customer confirms a purchase and reuses it for retries of that operation.If the application must continue the operation after restarting, it needs to retain the identifier with the pending operation.A fresh identifier generated for every attempt defeats the purpose.
A new confirmed purchase receives a new identifier, even if its items and address are identical.Hashing only the payload is therefore unsuitable as the complete definition of intention.Two equal shopping baskets can be two legitimate purchases.The contract needs an explicit distinction between semantic identity and identical content.AWS describes caller supplied request identifiers and their use in safe retries [2].This paper uses that documented principle as a starting point and proposes an order specific implementation.The service scopes an identifier to the authenticated customer and stores a digest of the normalized request.If the same customer reuses the identifier with a different quantity or delivery address, the service returns a content conflict.It must not silently accept the altered request or return the previous order as if the changes had been applied.Authentication remains necessary; knowledge of an identifier alone cannot authorize access to someone else's order.
3 State the local database invariant
The local design uses an intent record with customer scope, intent identifier, request digest, order identifier, and the information required to interpret the creation result. A unique constraint applies to the customer and intent pair. The proposed invariant is that a committed successful intent identifies exactly one committed order within this database boundary. In a first successful request, reservation of the identifier, creation of the order, and storage of the result occur in one transaction. Atomic commit provides the necessary all or nothing boundary for this local transition [3]. The schema and transaction still require implementation specific review.
An application level lookup is not a substitute for the unique constraint. Two workers can both observe that no intent exists and proceed concurrently. The database must arbitrate their competing writes. A worker that loses this competition should read the committed intent and interpret its result according to the contract. Details depend on isolation and conflict behaviour in the chosen database, so the implementation must test the actual engine. A generic claim that the code uses transactions is insufficient. The decisive question is whether every possible committed state preserves the relationship between the intent and its single order.
4 Trace the failure positions
First consider a process failure before the transaction begins. No business state has been committed, so a later attempt with the same identifier can execute normally. Next consider a failure during a transaction before commit. After recovery, the service must not retain a committed intent without its order or an order without the corresponding committed intent. Finally, consider successful commit followed by response loss. A retry must recover the original order reference and cannot create a second order. These are assertions derived from the proposed invariant. A real system must demonstrate them through its transaction and recovery behaviour.
A failure trace should state where observation is possible. The client sees a timeout, while the database can reveal whether the transaction committed. An operator may see a log entry written before commit that does not prove completion. The implementation should consequently distinguish received, committed, and responded events. These distinctions help diagnose incidents without treating a request log as an authoritative order ledger. Diagnostic events can be repeated or incomplete. The authoritative record is the committed business state within the defined boundary, interpreted with the operation identifier and the recorded request digest.
5 Replay has a business meaning
When a retry finds an existing successful intent, it should identify the order created by that operation. The response need not reproduce every timestamp or diagnostic field byte for byte. It must give the caller a semantically clear result. If the original order has subsequently been cancelled, repeating the historical creation operation should not create a replacement order. The interface can return the original order identifier and expose its current status separately. If current status and historical creation result share a response, their labels should prevent the customer from confusing a past successful creation with a currently active order.
An intent that is still being processed needs a specified response as well. The caller might receive a bounded wait, a pending result with a query route, or another documented contract. The choice depends on operational requirements. The important point is that concurrent execution must not be represented as an unrelated permanent business failure. Content conflicts are different from transient contention and should be reported differently. A request with the same identifier but a changed payload cannot be resolved by waiting for the old order. Clear distinctions let client code make safe decisions without inventing its own interpretation of ambiguous messages.
6 A hypothetical test matrix
For one test intent, launch twenty concurrent creation attempts with identical content. The primary assertion is that the database contains one matching order after all workers finish and recovery completes. Counting successful HTTP responses is secondary: several attempts may legitimately receive the same business result. Then submit identical content with a new intent identifier. A second order should be created, because the customer is expressing another purchase. Finally, reuse the first identifier with an altered quantity. The expected result is a content conflict and no change in order count. These tests check three different semantic requirements.
Fault injection should interrupt execution before reservation, after reservation but before commit, and after commit but before response delivery. The test environment must make those interruption points credible, rather than assuming that a random connection error reaches them. After each interruption, restart the service and repeat the same operation. Inspect the business invariant, result interpretation, and recovery time. The examples describe a proposed test plan; no twenty worker experiment has been performed for this paper. A report on an implementation would need its database version, isolation settings, test procedure, and retained failure evidence before presenting a reliability conclusion.
7 External payment is a separate boundary
The local transaction cannot atomically include an arbitrary remote payment service. A process can fail after creating an order and before sending a payment request, or after a remote charge and before recording its result locally. Order idempotency alone therefore cannot establish that a charge happens exactly once. The proposed system models payment as a separately identified operation and uses the payment service's documented duplicate detection or result query capability. If neither exists, repeated blind charging attempts can increase uncertainty rather than solve it. The local interface should retain a visibly unresolved state while reconciliation is performed.
One candidate architecture writes a pending event in the same local transaction as the order. A worker later reads that event and sends a payment operation with its own stable intent. Worker retries can produce duplicate deliveries, so the downstream contract must handle them. This architecture connects committed local state to eventual work, but it does not erase the downstream boundary. Reconciliation needs evidence about the remote business result, and any compensation needs its own authorization and retry rules. A system description should state these limits directly rather than placing an external side effect inside a box labelled transaction.
8 Retention and operational measurement
Intent retention should cover the supported retry window and plausible delayed requests. Removing a record while a valid delayed retry remains possible can permit a new order under an old intention. Indefinite retention has storage and data governance costs. The interface should specify how old intentions are handled, including whether an expired request is rejected and how a customer can query the existing purchase. The same rules should apply across routine cleanup and recovery from backup. A deletion schedule that is absent from the business contract can undermine an otherwise correct transaction design months after its initial tests.
Operational evidence should include duplicate order counts, content conflicts, pending outcomes, recovery duration, and the ability to reconcile an intent with its order. Identifiers in logs should support tracing without exposing unnecessary customer or payment data. A thousand test intentions with no duplicates would be useful evidence for that test set, but not a mathematical proof for every concurrency pattern and failure. A finite test report should identify which conditions were exercised and which remain untested. The local invariant supplies the reasoning target; tests reveal whether the implementation actually meets it under the specified conditions.
9 Conclusion
The proposed contract makes a purchase intention stable across uncertain delivery attempts and ties its local effect to a unique transactional record. Its logic fails if clients regenerate identifiers on retries, if competing workers bypass the constraint, or if the order and intent are committed separately. It also fails as a complete payment guarantee when remote effects are assumed to share a local transaction. These failure conditions are explicit enough to guide review and testing. An implementation can claim demonstrated behaviour only after exercising the invariant and recovery cases. Disabling a button improves interaction, but it supplies none of these server side guarantees.
References
[1] Fielding, R., Nottingham, M., and Reschke, J. (2022). HTTP Semantics. RFC 9110, Section 9.2.2. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html
[2] Featonby, M. Making retries safe with idempotent APIs. Amazon Builders' Library. https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/ Accessed 4 October 2026.
[3] SQLite. Atomic Commit In SQLite. https://www.sqlite.org/atomiccommit.html Accessed 4 October 2026.
